text: This lesson is about autonomous transactions — a real, genuinely unique PL-SQL capability for making a block's transaction completely independent of whatever transaction called it.

Here's the declaration: pragma autonomous transaction, right after the procedure header. It tells Oracle this block starts a brand new, fully independent transaction the moment it runs. It can commit or roll back entirely on its own, and neither action touches the calling transaction's pending work in any way.

And here's the real-world reason this exists: audit logging that survives a rollback. Log a login attempt as an autonomous transaction, and it commits immediately, independently. Then, if the main transfer later fails and rolls back, the audit row is already committed and survives regardless — exactly what an audit trail needs to do.

Oracle enforces one strict rule here: every autonomous block must end with an explicit commit or rollback before it returns control. Forget it, and Oracle raises O-R-A dash zero six five one nine and rolls the autonomous work back itself. There's no implicit commit on exit.

And T-SQL genuinely has nothing like this. Nested begin transaction calls in T-SQL are not independent — SQL Server just tracks a single nesting count, and an outer rollback undoes everything, including work that was logically inner. There's no T-SQL mechanism for a block to commit its own work irrevocably while a surrounding transaction is still pending.

Next lesson: BULK COLLECT and FORALL — the performance-oriented features PL-SQL gives you for cutting down the overhead of row by row processing, the same spirit as why a T-SQL developer prefers a set based insert select over a cursor loop. See you there.
